claim: A radio signal takes about 3 to 22 minutes one way between Earth and Mars, depending on where the two planets are in their orbits (some NASA pages round this to "4 to 24" or "5 to 20" minutes); between Earth and the Moon it takes about 1.3 seconds one way.

values.label: Earth-Mars one-way signal time, shortest (54.6 million km divided by the speed of light)
Earth-Mars one-way signal time, longest (401.4 million km divided by the speed of light)
Earth-Moon one-way signal time (384,400 km divided by the speed of light = 1.28 s)
Rounded range on the NASA Goddard page (2020)
Rounded range on the NASA Glenn slide deck (2021)

source_title: Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day (NASA Science, page last updated 10 Nov 2026)
quote: The distance between Earth and Mars changes as they orbit the Sun, and it can take anywhere from three minutes to 22 minutes for light to travel between the two planets.

extra_sources.title: Speaking Percy's Language: How to Talk so Perseverance Will Listen (NASA Science blog) - "between 3 and 22 minutes"
Space Communications: 7 Things You Need to Know (NASA Goddard, 6 Oct 2020) - "four to 24 minutes of latency"
Space Communications and Navigation, slide deck by NASA Glenn (NTRS 20210010148) - "about 5 to 20 minutes"
Hazard: Distance From Earth (NASA Human Research Program) - "communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way"
Mars Fact Sheet (NASA NSSDCA) - distance from Earth, minimum 54.6 and maximum 401.4 million km

notes: Draft said 4 to 24 minutes. That wording is real (NASA Goddard, 2020) but it does not match NASA's own distances: light needs 3.0 min at 54.6 million km and 22.3 min at 401.4 million km. Two NASA Science pages say 3 to 22 minutes, so use that. "5 to 20 minutes" is confirmed on a NASA Glenn slide deck: "It takes about 5 to 20 minutes for a radio signal to travel the distance between Mars and Earth, depending on planet positions". Moon: the same NASA light-day page says light "can traverse that distance in 1.3 seconds" (a question and its answer therefore take about 2.6 s).

claim: About every two years the Sun passes between Earth and Mars (Mars solar conjunction) and NASA stops sending commands to its Mars spacecraft for about two weeks: 2-16 October 2021, 11-25 November 2023, and most recently from 29 December 2025 until contact resumed on 16 January 2026 (about two and a half weeks).

values.label: Latest conjunction, contact with Mars missions resumes (NASA MAVEN blog)
Latest conjunction as described by the Curiosity team
Time between conjunctions (Mars synodic period, NASA fact sheet)

source_title: NASA's Mars Fleet Will Still Conduct Science While Lying Low (NASA/JPL, 10 Nov 2023)
quote: NASA will hold off sending commands to its Mars fleet for two weeks, from Nov. 11 to 25, while Earth and the Red Planet are on opposite sides of the Sun.

extra_sources.title: NASA's Mars Fleet Lies Low With Sun Between Earth and Red Planet (NASA/JPL, 28 Sep 2021)
NASA Works MAVEN Spacecraft Issue Ahead of Solar Conjunction (NASA Science blog, 23 Dec 2025)

Curiosity Blog, Sols 4788-4797: Welcome Back from Conjunction (NASA Science, 4 Feb 2026)
What's Mars Solar Conjunction, and Why Does It Matter? (NASA, 2019 conjunction)

notes: Core claim confirmed; the same 2023 release says "this phenomenon happens every two years". 2021 release: "most missions will stop sending commands between Oct. 2 and Oct. 16". There is no conjunction inside 2026 apart from the first half of January: the latest one ran over New Year. NASA MAVEN blog: "Mars solar conjunction ... begins Monday, Dec. 29, and NASA will not have contact with any Mars missions until Friday, Jan. 16"; the Curiosity team wrote "this one will last from Dec. 27 to Jan. 20". I found no single NASA press release for 2025-26, so these dates are blog-level and it lasted longer than the usual two weeks. Rovers keep working on pre-loaded commands during the pause. The next conjunction is due about 26 months later; its dates were not checked.

notes: Tau 10.8 and both dates are confirmed on NASA pages. The 645 Wh -> 22 Wh pair is NOT on any NASA page I could find: it comes from NASA's 13 June 2018 press briefing (rover project manager John Callas) as reported by Space.com. NASA's own graphic caption gives slightly different same-day numbers: "The June 10, 2018, tau measurement (10.5) was higher than any previously measured on the Red Planet. Energy level on that day (21 watt-hours) was the lowest ever measured on Opportunity at that time." If every number must trace to nasa.gov, show 'about 21-22 Wh' for 10 June and avoid the 645 figure (or credit it to the press briefing). The rover needed tau below 2.0 to recharge.

claim: NASA reported on 20 June 2023 that the International Space Station's life-support system had reached 98% water recovery (up from 93-94%), turning urine, sweat and breath moisture back into drinking water; the station's oxygen is made by electrolysis - using electricity to split water into oxygen and hydrogen.

values.label: Water recovery before the Brine Processor Assembly

source_title: NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station (NASA, 20 June 2023)
quote: We have now demonstrated that we can reach total water recovery of 98%, thanks to the brine processor.

extra_sources.title: Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) reference page (NASA Marshall) - oxygen by electrolysis

notes: Confirmed. The quote is by Jill Williamson, ECLSS water subsystems manager. Electrolysis quote (NASA ECLSS page): "The oxygen generation assembly is composed of the cell stack, which electrolyzes, or breaks apart, water provided by the Water Recovery System, yielding oxygen and hydrogen as byproducts." The oxygen goes to the cabin; the hydrogen is vented or combined with exhaled carbon dioxide to make more water.

claim: NASA's standard design numbers for one astronaut per day are about 0.84 kg of oxygen, about 1.6 kg of drinking water (NASA's current standard asks for at least about 2.5 litres of drinkable water) and about 0.62 kg of dry food - roughly 1.8 kg of food as eaten once the water in it is counted - about 5 kg in all.

values.label: ISS water need for drinking, food preparation and hygiene ("about a gallon")

source_title: Design Rules for Life Support Systems (Harry Jones, NASA Ames Research Center, 33rd International Conference on Environmental Systems, NTRS 20040012725)
quote: The metabolic use of oxygen is 0.84 kg/day per crewmember, as shown in Table 2.

extra_sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Environmental Control & Life Support System, OCHMO-TB-002 Rev B (NASA, 2023)
NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Food and Nutrition, OCHMO-TB-013 (NASA, 2023)
NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station (NASA, 20 June 2023)

notes: Draft oxygen value confirmed. The table values (oxygen 0.84, food solids 0.62, water in food 1.15, food-preparation water 0.76, drinking water 1.62, total 4.99 kg) come from Tables 2 and 6 of the NASA Ames paper, which cites the classic NASA reference (Wieland) and assumes 2,677 kcal per day. The PDF is a scan and I read it as OCR text, so check the table by eye before printing. Newer NASA wording: "Astronauts need approximately 2.5 L of potable water for hydration per crewmember per day" (OCHMO-TB-002) and "an average of 12,698 kJ (3,035 kcal) per day" (NASA-STD-3001 [V2 7003]). ISS article: "Each crew member needs about a gallon of water per day for consumption, food preparation, and hygiene such as brushing teeth." The 2023 brief computes oxygen as 0.771 kg per day at rest and 1.083 kg per day with exercise, so 0.84 is a planning average.

Wording: NASA says "This is the first time a station-grown crop has officially been on the menu for station crew members" and "the first crop grown and consumed in NASA hardware" - avoid 'first plants ever eaten in space'. The lettuce eaten was Veggie's second crop; the first (2014) was sent to Earth for safety tests. Radishes: "On Nov. 30, 2020, NASA astronaut Kate Rubins harvested radish plants" and they "reach maturity in just 27 days". values.value: three men for about four days

source_title: Apollo 13: Mission Details (NASA, 8 July 2009)

notes: Confirmed. Same NASA page: "Mission control devised a way to attach the CM canisters to the LM system by using plastic bags, cardboard and to tape all materials carried on board" (the typo is NASA's). NASA History lists the parts as "a spacesuit's liquid cooled garment and inlet hose, plastic bags, a cue card from the flight plan and of course duct tape" - the cardboard was a flight-plan card. The fix was designed and tested on the ground by a team led by Ed Smylie, then built in space by Jack Swigert and Jim Lovell. NASA spells it both "mail box" and "mailbox".

claim: On the night of 29-30 August 2018 flight controllers noticed a slow air leak on the International Space Station; the crew traced it to a hole about 2 mm wide in the docked Soyuz MS-09 spacecraft, slowed it with Kapton tape and then sealed it with epoxy on a gauze wipe.
source_title: International Space Station Status (NASA Space Station blog, 30 Aug 2018, 11:20 a.m. EDT)
quote: The leak has been isolated to a hole about two millimeters in diameter in the orbital compartment, or upper section, of the Soyuz MS-09 spacecraft attached to the Rassvet module of the Russian segment.

extra_sources.title: International Space Station Status, later update the same day (NASA Space Station blog, 30 Aug 2018) - epoxy and gauze repair

notes: Confirmed. First post: "The rate of the leak was slowed this morning through the temporary application of Kapton tape at the leak site." Second post: "Soyuz commander Sergey Prokopyev of Roscosmos used epoxy on a gauze wipe to plug the hole identified as the leak source." The hole was in the part of the Soyuz that does not return to Earth, and NASA said the crew was never in danger.

claim: The space station's urine recycler (Urine Processor Assembly) once failed because astronauts lose bone in weightlessness, which puts extra calcium in their urine; the calcium formed solid crystals that clogged the distillation unit, and NASA fixed it by changing the treatment acid from sulfuric to phosphoric.
source_title: Preventing Precipitation in the ISS Urine Processor (Muirhead, Carter, Williamson, Chambers; NASA Marshall Space Flight Center; ICES 2017; NTRS 20170008985)
quote: This occurred because the calcium concentration in the crew urine was elevated in microgravity due to bone loss.

extra_sources.title: NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station (NASA, 2023) - how the urine and brine processors work today

notes: Optional item, confirmed from the NASA abstract: "The higher calcium concentration precipitated with sulfate from the pretreatment acid, resulting in a failure of the UPA due to the accumulation of solids in the Distillation Assembly." After the failure the unit ran at reduced recovery until the new phosphoric-acid pretreatment was developed. The abstract does not give the date of the failure, so do not print one.

claim: Sunsets on Mars look blue because the very fine dust in the air lets blue light through more easily and scatters it forward, so a blue glow stays close to the Sun while the rest of the sky looks yellow to orange.

values.label: First colour sunset recorded by Curiosity (sol 956)

source_title: What Do Sunrises and Sunsets Look Like on Mars? (NASA Science, 1 May 2019)
quote: The colors come from the fact that the very fine dust is the right size so that blue light penetrates the atmosphere slightly more efficiently

extra_sources.title: Sunset in Mars' Gale Crater (NASA Science; credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/Texas A&M Univ.; 9 May 2015)

notes: Confirmed. The speaker is Mark Lemmon of Texas A&M University, a Curiosity science team member. He continues: "When the blue light scatters off the dust, it stays closer to the direction of the Sun than light of other colors does. The rest of the sky is yellow to orange, as yellow and red light scatter all over the sky instead of being absorbed or staying close to the Sun." Same page: "Martian sunsets typically stand out for their distinctive blue color."

notes: Corrections to the draft: (1) the feed is real, NASA-hosted and used by NASA's own widget, and it answers with HTTP 200 and the header Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (a browser game can read it directly), but it is not a documented NASA API and it is NOT real-time: on 11 Nov 2026 the newest of 4,745 records was sol 4995 (25 Aug 2026), about 11 weeks old. Show the record's own Earth date, never 'today', and ship a saved copy as fallback (the file is 1.7 MB; values are strings and missing ones are "--"). (2) The data come from Spain's Centro de Astrobiologia; the feed's disclaimer says it "is provided by Centro de Astrobiologia (CAB) and is intended for outreach purposes only". (3) Credit line confirmed exactly as NASA/JPL-Caltech/CAB(CSIC-INTA). The old page mars.nasa.gov/msl/weather/ now redirects to a Curiosity instruments page. Use max_temp and min_temp for air temperature; max_gts_temp and min_gts_temp are ground temperatures and run warmer by day (up to about +20 degrees C). The medians above are my own statistics from the feed, not NASA statements.

claim: NASA is paying the company ICON $57.2 million (a contract running through 2028, under NASA's MMPACT project) to develop its Olympus construction system, which is meant to 3D-print landing pads, habitats and roads on the Moon out of local soil (regolith).
source_title: NASA, ICON Advance Lunar Construction Technology for Moon Missions (NASA Marshall, 29 Nov 2022)
quote: The new NASA SBIR Phase III award will support the development of ICON’s Olympus construction system, which is designed to use local resources on the Moon and Mars as building materials.

extra_sources.title: NASA Looks to Advance 3D Printing Construction Systems for the Moon and Mars (NASA, 1 Oct 2020)

notes: Confirmed. Naming: NASA writes 'Olympus construction system' ('Project Olympus' is ICON's own name for it), and MMPACT stands for Moon to Mars Planetary Autonomous Construction Technologies. Same release: "NASA has awarded ICON, located in Austin, a contract to develop construction technologies that could help build infrastructure such as landing pads, habitats, and roads on the lunar surface" and "The contract runs through 2028 and has a value of $57.2 million." The release says 'local resources' rather than 'regolith'; the 2020 article describes tests with lunar soil simulant. This is technology under development - nothing has been printed on the Moon yet.

notes: All three draft numbers confirmed. The Mars figures are rows of the NASA fact-sheet table ('Distance from Earth: Minimum (10^6 km) 54.6, Maximum (10^6 km) 401.4'), not a sentence. 54.6 million km is the smallest possible distance; at an ordinary close approach Mars is about 78 million km away. NASA's Moon Facts page adds a kid-friendly picture: 30 Earth-sized planets could fit between Earth and the Moon.
